newsitem.title: USA: Study shows school violence prevention program works.
newsitem.headline: Study shows school violence prevention program works.

text.p: A violence prevention program in some elementary schools succeeded in calming aggressive behavior among youngsters, researchers said Tuesday.

After monitoring 790 second- and third-grade students from 12 elementary schools in King County, Washington, which includes Seattle, researchers said those given the "Second Step" anti-violence curriculum displayed less aggression in the classroom, on the playground and in the cafeteria.

Second Step consists of 30 lessons, each about 35 minutes, once or twice a week. They train students to identify their own feelings and those of others, teach impulse control and help students develop strategies for coping with anger and tense situations.

"Though these results are encouraging, such interventions may need to be accompanied by other interventions in early childhood and adolescence to further reduce aggressive behavior," study author David Grossman of the University of Washington in Seattle wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

The behavioral changes were not detected by the children's parents or teachers but were noticed by trained observers who were not told the study's purpose. The researchers said teachers may not have witnessed aggressive behavior outside the classroom, while behavior at home was not monitored.

Mark Rosenberg from the National Center for Injury Prevention and Control at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta said in an accompanying editorial that teachers across the country would welcome any change.
"This modest positive effect may be the most we have any right to hope for from projects like this," Rosenberg wrote. "To expect more is unrealistic."
